query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 1–2 atomic percent boron during the alloy processing will lead to boron segregation at grain boundaries, thereby reinforcing the boundaries to prevent crack initiation and propagation while preserving the large caloric response of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but suffers from poor integrity and intergranular cracking.
generation.intervention: Incorporate approximately 1–2 atomic percent boron into the alloy during its synthesis process.
generation.conditions: Under the same applied magnetic field and pressure conditions used to elicit the caloric response, within the operational temperature and loading regimes where the original alloy is tested.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries of the high-entropy alloy.
generation.mechanism: The added boron preferentially segregates to the grain boundaries, enhancing their cohesion and reducing the local stress concentrations that nucleate cracks. This improved intergranular bonding mitigates crack propagation without disrupting the intrinsic high caloric performance, as the bulk phase remains largely unchanged.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the boron-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit improved mechanical integrity (evidenced by increased compressive and tensile strengths and reduced crack propagation) while maintaining a similar magnitude of caloric response under field/pressure cycles.
generation.baseline: The unchanged (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which has high caloric performance but suffers from poor mechanical integrity manifested by intergranular cracking.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under the operational conditions (applied-field, pressure, and temperature regimes) typical for caloric applications. Its effectiveness may be limited at extremes of temperature or under very high strain rates where different deformation or phase transformation mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in mechanical strength and the potential for any subtle impacts on the caloric response remain to be validated experimentally. There is uncertainty regarding the optimal boron content and its distribution at the grain boundaries in this specific alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloys: one set processed with the addition of 1–2 at% boron and a control set without boron. Process both sets under identical conditions and then subject samples to standardized mechanical tests (compressive/tensile) as well as caloric performance assessments under applied magnetic field and pressure-field operations.
measurements: Measure compressive and tensile strength and record crack initiation and propagation characteristics (using SEM or in situ imaging).
Evaluate the caloric response (e.g., temperature change under field/pressure cycling) for both sets.
Conduct microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM or atom probe tomography) to confirm boron segregation at grain boundaries.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >20% increase) in mechanical integrity (reduced cracking, increased strength) compared to the control, or if the caloric response is significantly degraded relative to the control alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Micro-mechanical testing of small-scale HEA pillars
cited_evidence.text: Focused Ga ion beams (FIB) were used to mill fine-scale pillars out of the obtained HEA films and microcompression tests were carried out using a nanoindenter. After compression a fraction of large pillars, above 1 μm in diameter, experience cracking at the top parts and cracks propagate along grain boundaries, showing intergranular fracture behaviour, but it only occurs under strains larger than ∼20% (Fig. 2a). The smaller pillars (Fig. 2b–d) exhibit more uniform deformation without any cracking, even at above 30% compressive strain, suggesting that the compressive ductility is significantly improved. Furthermore, the columnar-structured HEA pillars exhibit very high yield and flow strengths. A 580-nm Normal HEA pillar shows a yield strength of ∼5 GPa and a 580-nm IBAD HEA pillar exhibits a yield strength of ∼6.5 GPa (Fig. 2e), which is almost twice of that of the single-crystal HEA pillar with the same diameter and orientation (Supplementary Fig. 4) and six times of that of the bulk HEA. Astonishingly, we find that the smallest IBAD HEA pillars (∼70–100 nm in diameter) exhibit remarkably high yield strengths of ∼8–10 GPa.

This observation indicates that the carbide may preferentially absorb slightly more Cr from the grain boundary than that from the grain interior during nucleation and growth due to faster diffusion along the grain boundary.
